item.title: Road map set for ramping up development
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-11
Road map set for ramping up development China has laid out a top-level road map dedicated to accelerating the development of new quality productive forces, which officials and analysts said could better sustain long-term economic expansion as the world's second-largest economy shifts toward new growth drivers. The latest guidelines, jointly released on Friday by the Communist Party of China Central Committee and the State Council, China's Cabinet, place greater emphasis on sci-tech innovation and its closer integration with industry, as well as stronger institutional support. Developing new quality productive forces — a concept first proposed in 2023 — is "an intrinsic requirement and an important focus" of high-quality development, the guidelines say. Authorities have acknowledged emerging challenges in putting the concept into practice, including poorly planned investment, neglect of upgrades to traditional industries and insufficient attention to reform. To keep the process on the right track, the guidelines stress the importance of innovation-driven development, reform and measures tailored to local conditions, and following the approach of "establishing the new before abolishing the old", an official from the National Development and Reform Commission said when elaborating on the document. In line with those principles, the document sets out 19 measures in five areas, with technological innovation topping the agenda. Priorities include strengthening "original and disruptive innovation" and speeding up the commercialization of research findings. Companies are assuming a central role in innovation, with their research and development spending estimated to account for more than 77 percent of China's total in 2025, according to the National Bureau of Statistics. That is close to the level of developed economies. The guidelines seek to further strengthen that role, calling for the establishment of a corporate R&D reserve system and a higher rate of additional tax deductions for R&D expenses. Furthermore, corporate R&D projects that meet national strategic needs will be designated as national projects under established procedures, the guidelines say. Li Chao, chief economist at Zheshang Securities, said he sees room for the additional R&D tax deduction rate for technology companies to rise from 100 percent to 120 percent. The measures mark a major shift from government-led to business-led allocation of innovation resources, said Fu Yifu, a researcher at Jiangsu Su Merchants Bank. As companies assume a greater role in innovation, more targeted government intervention is required to strike the right balance between government and the market, the NDRC official said. Authorities should focus on correcting market failures and ensuring fair competition, while curbing wasteful spending and copycat projects. The push for technological innovation also goes hand in hand with efforts to upgrade China's industrial base. "Developing new quality productive forces involves not only fostering emerging and future industries but also upgrading traditional sectors," the NDRC official said. To that end, the guidelines back companies' use of digital, smart and green technologies to upgrade traditional industries, while seeking to foster new pillar industries and establish mechanisms to sustain investment growth and share risks in future industries. In particular, the document gives priority to advancing the "AI Plus" initiative to expand AI applications across sectors. It also stresses the need to establish systems for technology monitoring, risk alerts and emergency response to ensure that AI is "safe, reliable and controllable". The parallel focus on upgrading traditional industries and fostering new ones points to a more coordinated approach to industrial policy, offering a practical path for China to improve its economic structure while maintaining overall stability, said Fu from Jiangsu Su Merchants Bank. On the institutional front, the guidelines promote patient capital for early-stage technology ventures and support stock market listings by eligible technology companies. Researchers will also face fewer barriers to moving between universities, research institutes and businesses. Greater openness is also a key part of the innovation push, as major economies step up investment in frontier technologies. The guidelines encourage foreign venture capital firms to expand in China and support the development of global innovation networks. For Dekra, a German testing, inspection and certification company, China's advances in AI, digital and green technologies are underpinning its continued expansion in the country, said Kilian Aviles, executive vice-president of the company and head of its Asia-Pacific operations. Dekra has upgraded and expanded key laboratories in Shanghai, Suzhou in Jiangsu province, Guangzhou in Guangdong province and Hefei in Anhui province. China's technological advances are also enabling Dekra to "bring proven solutions developed in China to markets across the Asia-Pacific and beyond", Aviles said.

item.title: Saudi-led coalition vows firm response to airport attack
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-11
Saudi-led coalition vows firm response after deadly attack on Riyadh airport RIYADH -- The Saudi-led coalition in Yemen has vowed to respond firmly to a Houthi attack on a passenger terminal at King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh on Saturday that killed 12 people and injured 309 others. Coalition spokesperson Turki Al-Malki said early Sunday on social media platform X that the coalition's Joint Forces Command would respond firmly to what he described as a "terrorist attack" in accordance with international humanitarian law. In separate posts on Sunday, Al-Malki said the Saudi-led coalition had intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile and a drone launched by the Houthi group toward Saudi Arabia. The fatalities in the airport attack included four Saudi citizens and eight foreign residents -- two Bangladeshis and one each from the United States, Egypt, Jordan, Syria, Palestine and Sudan, according to the Saudi aviation authority. The authority said the injured were receiving treatment at several hospitals, with some in serious condition, and that airport operations had been temporarily suspended. The attack came as the Houthi group and Saudi Arabia continued exchanging strikes on major airports and other facilities. Three people were killed and 36 others injured in two separate attacks targeting Abha International Airport in southwestern Saudi Arabia and King Khalid International Airport on Tuesday and Wednesday, respectively. On Thursday, three Saudi citizens, including a pilot, were killed and several others of other nationalities were injured in two Houthi attacks targeting King Khalid International Airport. Houthi-run al-Masirah TV reported earlier on Saturday that Saudi Arabia launched a new wave of air and missile strikes across Houthi-held areas in Yemen, targeting Sanaa International Airport in the Houthi-held capital, areas near the strategic Bab al-Mandab Strait and several northern provinces. Also on Saturday, Yemen's government forces said that more than 1,150 Houthi fighters had been "neutralized" and over 180 military and logistical vehicles destroyed or damaged in over 1,900 strikes across multiple fronts in Yemen over the preceding 24 hours. The figures could not be independently verified. Yemen has been mired in conflict since late 2014, when the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa and much of the country's north. A Saudi-led coalition intervened in 2015 in support of the internationally recognized Yemeni government, now based in the southern port city of Aden. The renewed fighting marks a major escalation after a UN-brokered truce in 2022 largely halted major hostilities. US President Donald Trump said Saturday that the United States "may" join Saudi Arabia in striking the Houthi group. "We just found out about the recent attack. So we'll make a decision. We move very quickly," he told reporters on the South Lawn of the White House. UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres on Sunday strongly condemned Saturday's Houthi attack on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh. "Attacks on civilians and civilian infrastructure are a violation of international law. These attacks must cease immediately," he wrote on X.

item.title: Tim Cook makes first China visit since stepping down
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-11
Tim Cook makes first China visit since stepping down as Apple CEO Tim Cook appeared in Guangzhou, Guangdong province, on Saturday, marking his first trip to China since stepping down as Apple's chief executive and his first visit as executive chairman of the company's board of directors. His itinerary began with a visit to the set of a traditional Chinese Wing Chun film, where a crew was using iPhone 18 Pro smartphones to capture the ancient martial art. Coinciding with Cook's arrival, Apple disclosed that committed investment for its second China Clean Energy Fund has risen to $212 million. The fund has roughly doubled in size since Apple completed an initial $100 million anchor investment last year. The increase reflects commitments from additional Apple suppliers such as Sunwoda Electronic Co Ltd. The fund has completed preliminary investments supporting a 260-megawatt wind project in the Guangxi Zhuang autonomous region and a 50-megawatt wind project in Shandong province, both now under construction. Apple also announced that more than 95 percent of its direct manufacturing in China now runs on renewable energy, as part of its goal to achieve carbon neutrality across its entire carbon footprint by 2030. Cook's China trip is directly tied to the 2026 meeting of the Tsinghua University School of Economics and Management Advisory Board, scheduled for Oct 13–14 in Beijing. This year marks the board's 27th annual gathering, which Cook has chaired since October 2019. Ahead of the meeting, the school announced three new board members: Jensen Huang, founder and CEO of Nvidia; Lisa Su, chair and CEO of AMD; and Marc Pictet, senior managing partner of Switzerland's Pictet Group. The advisory board, established in October 2000, brings together senior leaders from multinational corporations and academic institutions to strengthen ties between the school and the global business community.

item.title: Math apocalypse is coming for humanity's brightest minds
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-11
The mathematical apocalypse is coming for humanity's brightest minds For centuries, mathematicians have occupied the penthouse of human intelligence. Their discipline was the ultimate sanctuary of reason, where brilliance was measured not by eloquence but by irrefutable logic. On Oct 6 OpenAI delivered an unsettling message to its occupants: the machines are moving in, showing the potential and ambition to own the building. The company unveiled full or partial solutions to 372 outstanding problems in mathematics and theoretical computer science, generating more than 700 documents. Its claims included progress on the Kakeya conjecture, important algorithms and even the formidable Riemann hypothesis. Artificial intelligence seems to be quietly trespassing on intellectual territory reserved for Fields medalists. The reaction was a mix of astonishment, bewilderment and indignation. Timothy Gowers, a Fields medalist from the United Kingdom, likened the approaching transformation to a tsunami visible from the beach. Terence Tao, another mathematical luminary of the United States, warned of "proof indigestion", where machines produce mathematical arguments faster than humans can verify, understand or absorb them. The Association for Human Mathematics was less restrained. In a statement criticizing OpenAI's mass release, it declared: "Releasing over 700 files at once is not a demonstration of scholarship, but a demonstration of power." It urged mathematicians to stop collaborating with the company and defend research centered on human understanding. Mathematics is not merely an industrial process for manufacturing correct answers. Its purpose is to illuminate why something is true, discover connections and develop ideas that others can understand. An opaque, hundred-page machine-generated proof may establish a result without advancing human comprehension. Worse, asking academics to scrutinize hundreds of such manuscripts transfers the costs of corporate competition to the scientific community. OpenAI's reluctance to disclose its model, prompts and complete computational procedures compounds the problem. Some results remain unverified; others have reportedly required correction. Mathematical certainty cannot be established by a corporate press release. Yet mathematicians should avoid mistaking today's limitations for permanent barriers. AI systems are improving at a pace that makes predicting their intellectual limits increasingly hazardous. What began as sophisticated pattern recognition has developed into sustained mathematical reasoning, parallel experimentation and increasingly autonomous problem-solving. Errors can be corrected, verification can be automated and even the ability to identify fruitful questions, still largely a human preserve, may not remain so. This makes OpenAI's announcement more consequential than a mere technological publicity stunt. After writers, artists, translators and social scientists, mathematicians must confront a question once considered beneath their professional dignity: What happens when a machine becomes better at the very activity that defines your intellectual worth? The implications extend far beyond academic careers. Mathematics underpins cryptography, financial markets, weapons systems, AI itself and much of modern science. An AI capable of discovering mathematical truths beyond human understanding could dramatically accelerate technological progress. It could also generate capabilities whose consequences are understood only after their deployment. That possibility becomes especially troubling given recent controversies surrounding the safety and behavior of advanced AI systems developed by US technology companies. Companies racing to demonstrate ever-greater intelligence have powerful commercial incentives to advance capabilities faster than safeguards. Mathematical brilliance is no guarantee of prudence. Nor does superior mathematical reasoning establish machine consciousness. Self-awareness remains a speculative possibility, not a demonstrated achievement. But an autonomous system need not become conscious to behave unpredictably, pursue defined objectives or gain influence beyond effective human control. Humanity has created an extraordinary instrument for extending its intelligence. It may also have created a rival to that intelligence. The distinction matters less if people gradually lose the ability to understand, evaluate or restrain what their machines produce. The mathematicians' dilemma is thus a microcosm of humanity's predicament. They are discovering that the highest achievements of human reasoning may no longer belong exclusively to humans. Whether this heralds an intellectual renaissance or an unprecedented surrender of control depends on decisions being made now. The tsunami is still offshore. The danger is that its architects are too busy measuring the wave's height to notice how little time remains to prepare.

item.title: Zheng Qinwen claims maiden WTA 1000 title at China Open
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-11
Zheng Qinwen claims maiden WTA 1000 title at China Open BEIJING -- China's Zheng Qinwen captured the women's singles title at the 2026 China Open on Sunday, defeating fourth-seeded Russian Mirra Andreeva 7-5, 6-4 in the final to claim her maiden WTA 1000 crown before breaking down in tears during an emotional celebration on home soil. "The feeling is incredible. Winning here in Beijing, in front of my home crowd, has always been one of my dreams," Zheng said after the match. The victory also made Zheng the first Chinese player to win the singles title at the China Open. "Today's match was extremely tough. Mirra is a great player, and she broke my serve right at the start," Zheng said. "I just had to take it one point at a time and keep telling myself to hang in there and never give up. After playing so many matches, I was physically and mentally exhausted. But playing in front of my home crowd gave me that extra strength to keep pushing through." "I want to congratulate Mirra on her outstanding achievement at Roland Garros this year. I never had a chance to congratulate you in person, so I want to do that now. Congratulations on reaching the final this week as well. You are such a young and talented player, and congratulations to you and your team on everything you've achieved," she added. Since winning Olympic gold at the Paris 2024 Games, a persistent right elbow injury has disrupted Zheng's career and required surgery in July 2025. Her ranking subsequently fell from a career-high No 4 in 2024 to as low as No. 160 in mid-June 2026. "I want to thank my team for supporting me throughout this journey. I've been through a very tough year, and I couldn't have done this without you. Last but not least, I want to thank all the sponsors, the referees, and all the staff who have worked so hard throughout the week. And thank you to all the fans for your incredible support. This title belongs to all of you, too!" The victory earned Zheng 1,000 ranking points and $1,151,380 in prize money, lifting her to No 23 in the live WTA rankings.

item.description:

A day as a craftsperson in China's porcelain capital Share - WeChat
What's it like to be a porcelain craftsperson for a day in Taoxichuan, Jingdezhen, Jiangxi province? Transformed from the former Universe Porcelain Factory, Taoxichuan keeps Jingdezhen's centuries-old ceramic heritage alive. From shaping clay to painting blue-and-white designs, every step brings this timeless craft to life. Watch the video and experience it firsthand.

item.title: The Long March: An enduring inspiration
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-11
Retracing the Long March: From the birthplace of 25,000 Li to a new journey In August 1936, in response to Mao Zedong's call, Red Army soldiers put pen to paper to recount their firsthand experiences of the Long March (1934–36). Their accounts were compiled into a book titled 25,000 Li, which was completed in Yan'an in 1937. Ninety years after the victory of the Long March, China Daily reporter Yan An visits Yan'an, the cradle of the Chinese revolution and the place where the book was completed, to explore how the Long March has become a source of inspiration for generations to come. The Long March: An Enduring Inspiration, a mini-documentary that pays tribute to the enduring spirit of the Long March, premieres online on Oct 12. Follow Yan An as she retraces the footsteps of the Red Army and explores what the Long March spirit means for those embarking on their own new journeys today.

item.title: Tibetan postman delivers Long March spirit across grasslands
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-10
Tibetan postman delivers Long March spirit across grasslands Share - WeChat
On wind-scoured grasslands where Red Army troops trekked 90 years ago during the Long March, ethnic Tibetan postman Lhalung Dorje brings postal service to remote herding communities in Sichuan province. He covers the 3,500-meter-high "Long March mail route" in Zoige county, braving blizzards and boggy marshland through all seasons. Over 19 years on the job, he has logged nearly 580,000 kilometers and delivered more than 5 million pieces of mail without a single mistake, embodying the Long March spirit as a tireless messenger across the grasslands.

item.title: Xi on carrying forward Long March spirit
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-10
Xi on carrying forward Long March spirit Share - WeChat
This year marks the 90th anniversary of the victory of the Long March, which lasted from 1934 to 1936. The arduous journey helped lay the foundation for the eventual victory of the Chinese revolution. President Xi Jinping has always stressed the importance of carrying forward the spirit of the Long March, which has become a powerful spiritual force inspiring the Chinese people to overcome difficulties and advance from victory to victory.
